In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

We begin this session with what we had reached in the tafsir of Juz' an-Naba', where we arrived at Surah al-Qari'ah.

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah 1-2], and so on to the end.

The basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is a verse of the Book of Allah that is recited at the beginning of every surah. According to the preponderant opinion among the scholars, it is not counted among the verses of the surah, neither in al-Fatihah nor elsewhere. The first verse of al-Fatihah is His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾; the second: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾; the third: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾; the fourth: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾; the fifth: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾; the sixth: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾; and the seventh: ﴿Not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾. However, it was not recited at the beginning of Surah at-Tawbah (Bara'ah), because this was not established from the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) from the Prophet (ﷺ). Thus the matter became unclear to them: is it the remainder of Surah al-Anfal or an independent surah? For this reason, they placed a separator instead of the basmalah.

Allah says here: ﴿The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ "Al-Qari'ah" is an active participle from (qara'a), and the meaning is: the one that strikes hearts and terrifies them. This occurs at the blowing of the Trumpet, as Allah says: ﴿And the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾ [an-Naml 87]. It strikes the hearts after striking the ears. This Striking Calamity is a great calamity, without parallel before it, and it is among the names of the Day of Resurrection, just as it is called al-Ghashiyah (the Overwhelming) and al-Haqqah (the Inevitable Reality).

As for His saying: ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾, the "ma" here is an interrogative used to express glorification and magnification; meaning: what is the Striking Calamity that is spoken of?!

﴿And what can make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah 3]. This is an addition in magnification, grandeur and awe; meaning: what has informed you about this Striking Calamity?! That is: how great it is, and how severe it is!

Then He explained when it will be, saying, may He be exalted, ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah 4]. That is: it will occur at that time, the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths, when they come out of their graves.

The scholars said: they will be like scattered moths. The moth, as you know, is those small flying creatures that crowd together around a fire at night. They are weak, they almost walk without guidance, they pile up on one another, and sometimes, out of their heedlessness, they fall into the fire without realising it. So people resemble the moth in its weakness, its bewilderment, its crowding, and its moving about without guidance.

And ﴿al-mabthuth﴾ means dispersed, spread out. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿They will come out from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar 7]. If you picture this scene, people coming out of their graves in this manner, you would picture a tremendous matter with no equal: all of the world, from Adam until the Hour is established, coming out as one man, at one moment, from these graves scattered across the eastern and western parts of the earth. And [they will come out] from places other than graves, such as one who was thrown into the depths of the sea and eaten by the fish, or one thrown into the wastelands of the earth and eaten by wild beasts, or the like. All of them will come out at once, moving and roaming over this earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 101, verse 5:

As for the mountains, these are those great, firmly fixed, solid mountains, and they will become ﴿like wool fluffed up﴾ [al-Qari'ah 5]. Al-'ihn (العِهْن) means wool, and al-manfush (الْمَنْفُوش) means scattered apart. Or al-'ihn is cotton, and the meaning is one. The important point is that they will become, after having been solid, strong and firmly rooted, like fluffed-up wool or cotton. And al-manfush (الْمَنْفُوش), as we have said, means scattered apart, whether you fluff it with your hand or with a carding bow. It becomes light and is blown about by the slightest wind. God Most High has said in another verse that the mountains will become scattered dust[[He meant the saying of God Most High: ﴿And the mountains will be thoroughly crushed to pieces, and they will become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 5-6].]], and here the Most High said: ﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 101, verse 6–11:

﴿Then as for one whose scales are heavy, (6) he will be in a pleasant life. (7) But as for one whose scales are light, (8) his refuge will be an abyss. (9) And what can make you know what that is? (10) It is a fierce Fire.﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 6–11] Allah, exalted is He, divides people into two categories:

The first category: those whose scales are heavy, namely, the one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds.

The second: those whose scales are light, namely, the one whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds, or the one who has no good deed at all, such as the disbeliever.

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then as for one whose scales are heavy, (6) he will be in a pleasant life.﴾ Al-'Ishah (life, livelihood) is derived from al-'aysh, which means life; one says: "'Āsha al-rajulu zamanan ṭawīlan," meaning he remained and lived for a long time. Here al-'Ishah is on the pattern of (fi'lah), so it denotes a state (hay'ah) and not a verbal noun. The verbal noun indicating a single instance is said as (ʿaysha), whereas when you say (ʿīsha) it is (fiʿlah), indicating a state, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"(Fa'lah) is for a single occurrence, like jalsah (a single sitting), and (fi'lah) is for a state (hay'ah), like jilsah (a manner of sitting)."

The meaning is that he is in a good and pleasant life.
As for ﴿rāḍiyah﴾ (pleasing), it has been said that it is an active participle used in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., "marḍiyyah" (pleasing/pleased with). It has also been said that it is an active participle of the relative type, i.e., possessing contentment (dhāt riḍā); both meanings amount to one. The meaning is that it is a good life, free of hardship, free of turmoil, free of fatigue, complete in every respect. This life—meaning the life in Paradise, may Allah make us and you among its people—is the life of which ﴿No fatigue touches them therein, nor are they ever expelled from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48]. They neither grieve nor fear, in the most luxurious life, the most pure state of mind, and the most joyful condition; so it is a pleasing life.

﴿But as for one whose scales are light, (8) his refuge will be an abyss.﴾ As for ﴿one whose scales are light﴾, we have said that it is the disbeliever who has no good deed at all, because the good deeds of the disbeliever are rewarded in this world and do not benefit him in the Hereafter; or it is a Muslim who is extravagant against himself and whose evil deeds are greater.

﴿His refuge will be an abyss.﴾ The word (umm) here means: his intended destination; that is, the one toward which he is headed is the Abyss (al-Hawiyah). Al-Hawiyah is one of the names of the Fire; meaning his ultimate end is the Fire of Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "umm" here is "the mother of the brain"; the meaning being that he is thrown into the Fire upon the top of his head, we ask Allah for safety. When a verse can bear two meanings, neither of which is preferred over the other and they are not contradictory, both meanings are adopted together, and it is said: he is thrown into the Fire upon the top of his head; and also: he has no refuge and no destination except the Fire.

﴿And what can make you know what that is?﴾ This is for the sake of magnifying and exalting this Abyss, and we seek refuge in Allah. It asks: what is it? Do you know what it is? Indeed it is a great thing; it is ﴿a fierce Fire﴾, in the utmost degree of heat. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed it has been given a preference over the fire of this world by sixty-nine parts."[[Al-Bukhari (3265) and Muslim (2843/30), with the wording of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your fire which the son of Adam kindles is one part of seventy parts of the heat of Hell." They said: "By Allah, it would be sufficient, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It has been given a preference over it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."]] If you reflect on all the fires of this world, whether the fire of firewood, paper, butane gas, or something even more intense, the fire of Hell is preferred over them by sixty-nine parts; we ask Allah for well-being.

* In this verse there is warning and caution regarding this Day, and that people do not fall outside two states: either a man whose good deeds outweigh, or a man whose evil deeds outweigh.

* Also in it: evidence that the Day of Resurrection has scales. Some texts have mentioned that it is a single scale (mīzān); so is it one or many?

Some scholars have said: it is one, and it is expressed in the plural only with regard to what is weighed, because deeds, both good and bad, are weighed in it, and the good deeds of this person and that person are weighed in it, and the good deeds of this nation and that other nation are weighed in it; so it is plural with respect to what is weighed, not with respect to the scale, which is one.

Other scholars have said: they are multiple scales; each nation has a scale, and each deed has a scale, and for this reason it is in the plural.

The more apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that it is one scale, but it is expressed in the plural with regard to what is weighed, according to the deeds, or according to the nations, or according to the individuals.

* And in this verse: evidence that when a person's good deeds and evil deeds are equal, he is passed over in silence in this verse; but Allah, exalted is He, has made clear in Surah al-A'raf that they do not enter the Fire, but are held back in a place called al-A'raf. Allah, exalted is He, mentions in Surah al-A'raf what takes place between them and the believers, and that ﴿when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people"﴾ [al-A'raf: 47]. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to make us and you among those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds, to forgive us and you, to deal with us in His pardon; indeed He is Able over all things.

(10) It is a fierce Fire.﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 6–11] Allah, exalted is He, divides people into two categories:

The first category: those whose scales are heavy, namely, the one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds.

The second: those whose scales are light, namely, the one whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds, or the one who has no good deed at all, such as the disbeliever.

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then as for one whose scales are heavy, (6) he will be in a pleasant life.﴾ Al-'Ishah (life, livelihood) is derived from al-'aysh, which means life; one says: "'Āsha al-rajulu zamanan ṭawīlan," meaning he remained and lived for a long time. Here al-'Ishah is on the pattern of (fi'lah), so it denotes a state (hay'ah) and not a verbal noun. The verbal noun indicating a single instance is said as (ʿaysha), whereas when you say (ʿīsha) it is (fiʿlah), indicating a state, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"(Fa'lah) is for a single occurrence, like jalsah (a single sitting), and (fi'lah) is for a state (hay'ah), like jilsah (a manner of sitting)."

The meaning is that he is in a good and pleasant life.
As for ﴿rāḍiyah﴾ (pleasing), it has been said that it is an active participle used in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., "marḍiyyah" (pleasing/pleased with). It has also been said that it is an active participle of the relative type, i.e., possessing contentment (dhāt riḍā); both meanings amount to one. The meaning is that it is a good life, free of hardship, free of turmoil, free of fatigue, complete in every respect. This life—meaning the life in Paradise, may Allah make us and you among its people—is the life of which ﴿No fatigue touches them therein, nor are they ever expelled from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48]. They neither grieve nor fear, in the most luxurious life, the most pure state of mind, and the most joyful condition; so it is a pleasing life.

﴿But as for one whose scales are light, (8) his refuge will be an abyss.﴾ As for ﴿one whose scales are light﴾, we have said that it is the disbeliever who has no good deed at all, because the good deeds of the disbeliever are rewarded in this world and do not benefit him in the Hereafter; or it is a Muslim who is extravagant against himself and whose evil deeds are greater.

﴿His refuge will be an abyss.﴾ The word (umm) here means: his intended destination; that is, the one toward which he is headed is the Abyss (al-Hawiyah). Al-Hawiyah is one of the names of the Fire; meaning his ultimate end is the Fire of Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "umm" here is "the mother of the brain"; the meaning being that he is thrown into the Fire upon the top of his head, we ask Allah for safety. When a verse can bear two meanings, neither of which is preferred over the other and they are not contradictory, both meanings are adopted together, and it is said: he is thrown into the Fire upon the top of his head; and also: he has no refuge and no destination except the Fire.

﴿And what can make you know what that is?﴾ This is for the sake of magnifying and exalting this Abyss, and we seek refuge in Allah. It asks: what is it? Do you know what it is? Indeed it is a great thing; it is ﴿a fierce Fire﴾, in the utmost degree of heat. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed it has been given a preference over the fire of this world by sixty-nine parts."[[Al-Bukhari (3265) and Muslim (2843/30), with the wording of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your fire which the son of Adam kindles is one part of seventy parts of the heat of Hell." They said: "By Allah, it would be sufficient, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It has been given a preference over it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."]] If you reflect on all the fires of this world, whether the fire of firewood, paper, butane gas, or something even more intense, the fire of Hell is preferred over them by sixty-nine parts; we ask Allah for well-being.

* In this verse there is warning and caution regarding this Day, and that people do not fall outside two states: either a man whose good deeds outweigh, or a man whose evil deeds outweigh.

* Also in it: evidence that the Day of Resurrection has scales. Some texts have mentioned that it is a single scale (mīzān); so is it one or many?

Some scholars have said: it is one, and it is expressed in the plural only with regard to what is weighed, because deeds, both good and bad, are weighed in it, and the good deeds of this person and that person are weighed in it, and the good deeds of this nation and that other nation are weighed in it; so it is plural with respect to what is weighed, not with respect to the scale, which is one.

Other scholars have said: they are multiple scales; each nation has a scale, and each deed has a scale, and for this reason it is in the plural.

The more apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that it is one scale, but it is expressed in the plural with regard to what is weighed, according to the deeds, or according to the nations, or according to the individuals.

* And in this verse: evidence that when a person's good deeds and evil deeds are equal, he is passed over in silence in this verse; but Allah, exalted is He, has made clear in Surah al-A'raf that they do not enter the Fire, but are held back in a place called al-A'raf. Allah, exalted is He, mentions in Surah al-A'raf what takes place between them and the believers, and that ﴿when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people"﴾ [al-A'raf: 47]. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to make us and you among those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds, to forgive us and you, to deal with us in His pardon; indeed He is Able over all things.
